subject: chemistry
question_text: Define wave number. Give its unit.

verification.note: PREDICTED, not asked. This question is not listed in the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section; it comes from the enumeration sweep of the Atomic Structure syllabus against the standard question archetypes. Both the question and the 1+1 mark split are claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Wave number is the number of waves present
It is written as ν̄ (nu bar).
steps.why: Wave number counts waves per unit length, so it is a way of measuring a wave by how tightly packed it is rather than by how long each wave is. Spectroscopy uses it because the numbers come out convenient.
common_mistakes: Defining wave number as the number of waves per second. That is the frequency.
Writing ν instead of ν̄. The bar matters.
steps.memory_tip: Frequency counts waves per second. Wave number counts waves per centimetre.
steps.margin_note: Write the symbol with its bar. Examiners look for it.

steps.label: The relation and unit
lines: Unit: cm⁻¹ (also m⁻¹ in the SI system)
Since ν = c / λ, it follows that ν = c ν̄
steps.why: Wave number is simply the reciprocal of the wavelength, so a short wave gives a large wave number. Because energy rises with wave number through E = hcν̄, spectral lines are often listed directly in cm⁻¹.
common_mistakes: Giving the unit as cm. Wave number is a count per length, so the unit is cm⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Reciprocal of wavelength, so the unit is a reciprocal length: cm⁻¹.
steps.margin_note: The unit is half of this mark. Never leave it out.

insider_note: The question asks for the unit outright, and the second mark carries the relation and the unit together. A definition alone, however well written, is capped at one of the two marks.
